record.original_question: Does the finite repetition threshold on four letters equal the usual repetition threshold, i.e. is FRT(4) = RT(4) = 7/5?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
For a finite alphabet $A$, the exponent of a finite nonempty word $w$ is $|w|/p(w)$, where $p(w)$ is the smallest period of $w$. For an infinite word $\mathbf{w}$, let $E(\mathbf{w})$ denote the supremum of the exponents of its finite factors. The repetition threshold on $k$ letters is
$$\mathrm{RT}(k) = \inf\{ E(\mathbf{w}) : \mathbf{w} \text{ is an infinite word over an alphabet of size } k \}.$$
By Dejean's theorem, $\mathrm{RT}(4) = 7/5$. The finite repetition threshold on $k$ letters, $\mathrm{FRT}(k)$, is defined as the infimum of the real numbers $r$ such that there exists an infinite word $\mathbf{w}$ over an alphabet of size $k$ with $E(\mathbf{w}) \le r$ and such that $\mathbf{w}$ has only finitely many distinct factors of exponent equal to $\mathrm{RT}(k)$.

Determine whether $\mathrm{FRT}(4) = \mathrm{RT}(4) = 7/5$.
artifact.status_search_result: The equality FRT(4) = RT(4) = 7/5 is established: there exists an infinite Dejean word over a 4-letter alphabet (avoiding factors of exponent greater than 7/5) containing only finitely many (in fact two) factors of exponent exactly 7/5. This was shown in work on finite-repetition thresholds for large alphabets following the ternary case.

status_evidence.title: Finite repetition threshold for large alphabets
status_evidence.snippet: There exists an infinite Dejean word on a 4-letter alphabet containing only two 7/5-powers, hence FRT(4) = 7/5.

status_evidence.title: Finite-Repetition threshold for infinite ternary words
status_evidence.snippet: Introduces the finite-repetition threshold and proves results for ternary alphabets, conjecturing equality with the repetition threshold.
status_evidence.claim: Source defining FRT and resolving early cases, with subsequent work confirming FRT(4)=7/5.
